newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Investors look for Balkan opportunities.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Investors look for Balkan opportunities.

text.p: The turmoil in the Balkans may add to the old stereotype of the region as the powder-keg of Europe, yet for some investors it could be the chance for unexpected opportunities.
"Everyone is scrambling around looking for the next big hit, the next success story," said a U.S. fund manager, who asked not to be named, referring to increased foreign buying in Romanian stocks.
Still on the sidelines himself because that market is too shallow for his multi-billion dollar fund, he believes he would be in Romania within the next six months at best or two years at worst.

The reason for cautious optimism at a time of chaos and near civil war in Albania, the still unsettled situation in Bosnia and abundant economic disasters throughout the region, are the positive developments in some of its key countries.

On the back of popular discontent, reform-minded politicians managed to replace ineffective governments in Bulgaria and Romania. In Serbia, the once weak opposition has made inroads into the structures of power and looks set to win national elections later this year.
"This has been a winter of Balkan discontent," said David Boren, vice president, Emerging Market Research, at Salomon Brothers in London.

He said the people of Romania, Bulgaria and Serbia had inspired each other to seek political and economic change. He doubted the trouble in Albania could discourage investors from the region as a whole.

Analysts recognise the risk that the new enthusiasm for reform will be squandered once again, but they point out that never before have all the elements needed for success been in place at the same time.
SHOCK-THERAPY BACK ON AGENDA

Many of the region's economic problems stem from the way in which countries emerged from decades of communism. Reformers often inherit economies in a worse state than they were back in the early 1990s.

The core of the former East Bloc countries pursued vigorous political and economic reforms from the start, but most of their southern neighbours wasted the initial momentum for change, applying half-measures and often concentrating on the transfer of state wealth to private hands.

Many countries are now introducing strict austerity measures and seeking financial help from the International Monetary Fund and the European Union to re-launch economic reforms. Wide-scale privatisation is on the cards, auguring well for equity investors.
But Serbia and Albania, although taking their economic problems seriously, seem for some time to come unable to pursue adequate economic reform because of astute political crises.

The former Yugoslav republics of Slovenia and Croatia, cherishing an investment grade status, are already attracting considerable investment. They are perceived as belonging to the core emerging markets than the Balkan fold.
ROMANIA MAY BE THE NEXT STAR
"Romania's economy is more stable at the present time and it has the advantage over Bulgaria because the immediate crisis isn't that severe," said Salomon's Boren.

Analysts are impressed with the vigour with which the new authorities in Bucharest started their overhaul of the crumbling economy. The liberalisation of the foreign exchange market, tight fiscal and monetary policy and privatisation plans have won the new government of Prime Minister Victor Ciorbea support from the IMF and investor confidence. But it is clear the shock therapy will hurt growth in the short-term, making especially equity investment a risk.

The nascent equity market is going though a mini-boom, however, driven by hedge funds and more mobile investors. Even more cautious, large investment funds predict greater foreign inflows once the shock-therapy shows signs of bringing recovery.

"Money will flow in at the end of the day. There may be fundamental problems but the story will look interesting on the funds flow basis," said the fund manager who recently returned from a fact-finding mission in Romania. He said the main barriers at the moment were extremely low liquidity and lack of reliable valuations and accounting practices.
Analysts said some firms seemed to be trading at a fraction of their published book value but the real quality of assets was hard to determine.

Other impediments include currency risk after the leu was liberalised -- although a crawling peg system is expected to be implemented to give it stability -- and a lack of regulations allowing free profit repatriation and foreign participation in the market. The government is already working to dismantle such obstacles.

On the debt side, Romania is poised to tap international markets quite frequently, with this year's borrowing plans at about $1.6 billion. A $500 million Eurobond issue is planned within the next two months, and analysts predict they can be priced between 250-300 basis points over U.S. treasuries.

The relatively good pricing taking into account the state of the economy, reflects not only confidence in Romania's recovery, but the generally low level of its current indebtedness. The external debt is running at roughly 20 percent of gross domestic product.
Some analysts expect the spreads on existing Romania Eurobonds to tighten to 230 basis points in the next 12 months.
HOPES OF IMF HELP IN BULGARIA

Investors were snatching up Bulgaria's Brady bonds some three weeks ago, believing that the country's economic decline hit bottom and its new reform-minded government will strike a quick accord with the IMF and move fast with much-delayed structural reforms.

Progress was lower than expected in talks between Sofia and an IMF delegation last week and some foreign investors are worried that the new government, unlike in Romania, is trying to bargain too hard with the Fund.
"I'm disappointed that the interim government did not agree to everything what the IMF wanted," said Andrew Kenningham, senior analyst at Merrill Lynch.

The main bone of contention seems to be the fate of the collapsing banking system, with the Fund pushing for the quick sale of four banks and subjecting two others to foreign management. The government opposes the plan, saying it wants to keep the banks under current management, re-capitalise them with foreign money and sell them later. Many analysts support the IMF view, saying a quick overhaul of the banking sector was crucial to restore confidence in the lev currency and to avoid further bad debt pile-up.

A deal with the IMF, envisaging a currency board regime for the lev, quick privatisation, closures of top loss-making firms and opening the economy up to foreign investment would unlock some $700 million from the Fund and pave the way to crucial aid from the World Bank and European Union. The money is essential not only to help kick-off the painful reforms but to allow Bulgaria to service its external debt. The next coupon payment on the Bradys is due in July and there are some residual fears that the country may default.

The Bulgarian Bradys were trading at around 850 basis points over U.S treasuries last week and even though some analysts see them gaining to the 600 points level as soon as the IMF deal is struck, others say the outlook is neutral. They say this view is based on the enormous task awaiting the government and add that it remains to be seen if the government is after all prepared to follow the IMF line more closely.
"The question in Bulgaria is 'Is it not too late?'," said Salomon's Boren. "If they don't undergo a significant economic turnaround, they are going to face a complete financial collapse."
He said, however, that the market has bet on the ultimate success in Bulgaria.

Apart from external debt, the expected development of domestic debt markets should offer opportunities as well, if the turnaround comes, thanks to the combination of a fixed exchange rate under the currency board and high nominal interest rates.
RUMP-YUGOSLAVIA HAS POTENTIAL

In stark contrast to Slovenia and Croatia, foreigners keep a safe distance from other ex-Yugoslav states. But they closely monitor the situation there, waiting for political change in Serbia and for Bosnia and Macedonia to make further progress in reforms.
"They are just blips on the radar now, too speculative to enter," one fund manager said.
But if the Serbian opposition wins this year's election and the Socialists loose power, investing in the relatively modern Yugoslav economy would be compelling, analysts say.

"It is essentially a modern economy with a European orientation and the potential for market developments in the financial sector and elsewhere could under a different regime be attractive," said Boren.

At the moment the economy is looking into an abyss and will require a radical IMF-backed reform package. The main areas that need to be addressed are re-capitalising cash-starved enterprises, and freeing the economy, especially banks, from political patronage. This can be achieved by privatisation and making the central bank fully independent, but it remains to be seen how much even the Serbian opposition, if it wins power, is ready to listen and follow IMF advice.
